content: Diarrhetic shellfish poisoning (DSP) is one of the four recognized types of shellfish poisoning, alongside paralytic shellfish poisoning, neurotoxic shellfish poisoning, and amnesic shellfish poisoning. The primary symptom of DSP is diarrhea, although other symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps are also frequently observed. Symptoms of DSP typically begin approximately 30 minutes after consuming contaminated shellfish and generally resolve within 24 hours. The condition is caused by a toxin known as okadaic acid. This toxin inhibits the phosphorylation processes within intestinal cells, leading to increased permeability of these cells to water. As a result, individuals experience severe diarrhea, which carries a risk of dehydration. Despite the severity of the symptoms, DSP does not typically result in life-threatening complications. To date, no fatalities have been reported as a consequence of this condition.
